In [[algebraic topology]], a '''fiber-homotopy equivalence''' is a map over a space ''B'' that has homotopy inverse over ''B'' (that is if <math>h_t</math> is a homotopy between the two maps, <math>h_t</math> is a map over ''B'' for ''t''.) It is a relative analog of a [[homotopy equivalence]] between spaces.

Given maps ''p'': ''D'' → ''B'', ''q'': ''E'' → ''B'', if ƒ: ''D'' → ''E'' is a fiber-homotopy equivalence, then for any ''b'' in ''B'' the restriction
:<math>f: p^{-1}(b) \to q^{-1}(b)</math>
is a homotopy equivalence. If ''p'', ''q'' are fibrations, this is always the case for homotopy equivalences by the next proposition.

{{math theorem
 |name=Proposition
 |math_statement=<ref>{{harvnb|May|1999|loc=Ch 7., § 5.}}</ref> Let <math>p: D \to B, q: E \to B</math> be [[fibration]]s. Then a map <math>f: D \to E</math> over ''B'' is a [[homotopy equivalence]] if and only if it is a fiber-homotopy equivalence.
}}

There is also a completely analogous notion of a '''cofiber-homotopy equivalence''', a homotopy equivalence such that the homotopies connecting the compositions and the identities are homotopies under the base. Then, similar to the above, we have:

{{math theorem
 |name=Proposition
 |math_statement=<ref>{{harvnb|May|1999|loc=Ch 6., § 5.}}</ref> Let <math>i: A \to X, j : A \to Y</math> be [[cofibration]]s. Then a map <math>f: X \to Y</math> under ''A'' is a [[homotopy equivalence]] if and only if it is a cofiber-homotopy equivalence.
}}

== Proof of the proposition ==
The following proof is based on the proof of Proposition in Ch. 6, § 5 of {{harv|May|1999}}. We write <math>\sim_B</math> for a homotopy over ''B''.

We first note that it is enough to show that ƒ admits a left homotopy inverse over ''B''. Indeed, if <math>g f \sim_{B} \operatorname{id}</math> with ''g'' over ''B'', then ''g'' is in particular a homotopy equivalence. Thus, ''g'' also admits a left homotopy inverse ''h'' over ''B'' and then formally we have <math>h \sim f</math>; that is, <math>f g \sim_{B} \operatorname{id}</math>.

Now, since ƒ is a homotopy equivalence, it has a homotopy inverse ''g''. Since <math>fg \sim \operatorname{id}</math>, we have: <math>pg = qfg \sim q</math>. Since ''p'' is a fibration, the homotopy <math>pg \sim q</math> lifts to a homotopy from ''g'' to, say, ''g<nowiki>'</nowiki>'' that satisfies <math>pg' = q</math>. Thus, we can assume ''g'' is over ''B''. Then it suffices to show ''g''ƒ, which is now over ''B'', has a left homotopy inverse over ''B'' since that would imply that ƒ has such a left inverse.

Therefore, the proof reduces to the situation where ƒ: ''D'' → ''D'' is over ''B'' via ''p'' and <math>f \sim \operatorname{id}_D</math>. Let <math>h_t</math> be a homotopy from ƒ to <math>\operatorname{id}_D</math>. Then, since <math>p h_0 = p</math> and since ''p'' is a fibration, the homotopy <math>ph_t</math> lifts to a homotopy <math>k_t: \operatorname{id}_D \sim k_1</math>; explicitly, we have <math>p h_t = p k_t</math>. Note also <math>k_1</math> is over ''B''.

We show <math>k_1</math> is a left homotopy inverse of ƒ over ''B''. Let <math>J: k_1 f \sim h_1 = \operatorname{id}_D</math> be the homotopy given as the composition of homotopies <math>k_1 f \sim f = h_0 \sim \operatorname{id}_D</math>. Then we can find a homotopy ''K'' from the homotopy ''pJ'' to the constant homotopy <math>p k_1 = p h_1</math>. Since ''p'' is a fibration, we can lift ''K'' to, say, ''L''. We can finish by going around the edge corresponding to ''J'':
:<math>k_1 f = J_0 = L_{0, 0} \sim_B L_{0, 1} \sim_B L_{1, 1} \sim_B L_{1, 0} = J_1 = \operatorname{id}.</math>
